Exercise 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

ggplot(college_grad_df, aes(x = median)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2500, colour = "black",
                 fill = "skyblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Median Earnings",
    x = "Median Earnings ($)",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

college_grad_df %>%
  group_by(major_category) %>%
  summarise(
    median_earnings = median(median, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_earnings = mean(median, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(median_earnings))
## # A tibble: 16 × 3
##    major_category                      median_earnings mean_earnings
##    <chr>                                         <dbl>         <dbl>
##  1 Engineering                                   57000        57383.
##  2 Computers & Mathematics                       45000        42745.
##  3 Business                                      40000        43538.
##  4 Physical Sciences                             39500        41890 
##  5 Social Science                                38000        37344.
##  6 Biology & Life Science                        36300        36421.
##  7 Law & Public Policy                           36000        42200 
##  8 Agriculture & Natural Resources               35000        36900 
##  9 Communications & Journalism                   35000        34500 
## 10 Health                                        35000        36825 
## 11 Industrial Arts & Consumer Services           35000        36343.
## 12 Interdisciplinary                             35000        35000 
## 13 Education                                     32750        32350 
## 14 Humanities & Liberal Arts                     32000        31913.
## 15 Arts                                          30750        33062.
## 16 Psychology & Social Work                      30000        30100

Your explanation The distribution of median earnings is expected to be positively skewed which means it mainly lies on the left side of the graph. This means that most college majors have median earnings concentrated around the lower-to-middle part of the distribution, while a smaller number of majors have considerably higher median earnings. From the Table we can see that the major catergory with highest median earnings is engineers. # Exercise 2: Exploring relationship

ggplot(college_grad_df,
       aes(x = sharewomen, y = median)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              colour = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Median Earnings vs Share of Women",
    x = "Share of Women",
    y = "Median Earnings ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

Your explanation a. The variables are median which is the response variable and the second variable is sharewomen which is the explanatory variable.

  1. The scatterplot allows us to examine the relationship between the proportion of women in a major and its median earnings. In the graph we can see a clear direction: downward sloping regression line which would indicate a negative association, suggesting that majors with a higher proportion of women tend to have lower median earnings. The magnitude is how closely the dots are clustered around the line of best fit.

Exercise 3: Fit and interpret a numerical predictor

share_fit <- lm(median ~ sharewomen,
                data = college_grad_df)
summary(share_fit)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = median ~ sharewomen, data = college_grad_df)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -17261  -5474  -1007   3502  57604 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)    56093       1705   32.90   <2e-16 ***
## sharewomen    -30670       2987  -10.27   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 9031 on 170 degrees of freedom
##   (1 observation deleted due to missingness)
## Multiple R-squared:  0.3828, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3791 
## F-statistic: 105.4 on 1 and 170 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
coef(share_fit)
## (Intercept)  sharewomen 
##    56093.31   -30669.94
share_aug <- augment(share_fit)
ggplot(share_aug,
       aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs Predicted Values",
    x = "Predicted Median Earnings",
    y = "Residuals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Your explanation a. Interpret is when predicted earnings when share of women is 0. Predicted Median equals 56093 - 30670 share of women. b.The residual plot is used to assess whether a linear model is appropriate. If the residuals are randomly distributed around zero without a clear pattern.

Exercise 4: Consider a categorical variable instead

college_grad_df <- college_grad_df %>%
  mutate(
    engineering = if_else(
      major_category == "Engineering",
      "Engineering",
      "Other"
    )
  )
engineering_fit <- lm(
  median ~ engineering,
  data = college_grad_df
)
summary(engineering_fit)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = median ~ engineering, data = college_grad_df)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -17383  -4681  -1681   3319  52617 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)         57383       1574   36.46   <2e-16 ***
## engineeringOther   -20702       1725  -12.00   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 8476 on 171 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4571, Adjusted R-squared:  0.454 
## F-statistic:   144 on 1 and 171 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
levels(factor(college_grad_df$engineering))
## [1] "Engineering" "Other"
view(college_grad_df)

Your explanation Baseline will be engineering as E comes before O. Average median for engineering majors is 57383 which is the intercept. and the slope would be -20702. —
